goal.text: Close the ten confirmed root causes recorded on ai-orchestrator issue 30, across the four repositories that own them, so that the harness stops losing dispatches to an unpinned toolchain, an unbounded simulated supervisor, a monitor killed for a correct quiet turn, a liveness proof that decays, a stop that lies, a publication verified by the wrong working tree, a run journal that goes blind on codex, and advice that contradicts the state it is printed under.

tasks.title: fix(nx): run the workspace's pinned Nx and settle what the shared cache does

steps.task:
## What

`scripts/nx.sh` line 61 invokes `bunx nx "$@"`. `bunx` resolves and installs Nx per
invocation and extracts its ~22 MB native binary into a fresh
`/tmp/nx-native-file-cache-<hash>` directory that nothing ever removes. On this host that
family reached 5,245 directories totalling ~113 GiB while holding roughly 44 MB of unique
content — one binary copied thousands of times, not a cache of workspace data. A version
census across it found 2,179 invocations on Nx 23.1.0 against 2,949 on Nx 23.1.1, while
`package.json` pins `"nx": "23.1.0"` exactly: the majority of Nx invocations on this host
ran a version the lockfile does not pin, which is the precise failure a frozen-lockfile
install exists to prevent.

Make the wrapper run the workspace's own pinned Nx binary. `node_modules/.bin/nx` already
exists at the pinned version, and `scripts/workspace-install.sh` — which this wrapper runs
two lines earlier and which reconciles the installed tree against the lockfile rather than
merely checking a binary is present — guarantees it before every run.

**Four sibling repositories have already made this change, and they are the reference
implementation rather than a design to derive.** Read one before writing this one:
`/home/nick/.ai-orchestrator/repos/nickderobertis__onepipeline/scripts/nx.sh`, and the
same file under `nickderobertis__onevcs`, `nickderobertis__oneagentgraph` and
`nickderobertis__onepipeline-ui`. Each resolves `NX_BIN="node_modules/.bin/nx"` with a
`.cmd` fallback and refuses when neither exists. Follow that shape where it fits; this
wrapper has two things they do not — the preserved log and the shared cache key — and
neither should change here.

Add a drift check to this repository's suite that fails when the Nx the wrapper actually
runs is not the version `package.json` pins, so a regression is a red check rather than
silent accumulation. Assert it from what the wrapper runs, not from the script's text: the
text is what was already true when the version drifted.

## Why

The disk reached 91% with 17 GiB free and removing this one family reclaimed 108 GB,
leaving 125 GiB free — and a full disk on this host does not announce itself, it announces
itself as unrelated tests failing. The reproducibility half is the more damaging one and is
the same shape as the `onepipeline-ui` incident this repository already records, where six
defects were filed against a bundle that had already shipped them fixed: a gate that runs
an unpinned toolchain returns a verdict about a tree the lockfile does not describe.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Nx wrapper runs the Nx binary the workspace lockfile pins, and no path through it resolves or installs Nx from the network.
- A wrapper invocation in a checkout whose installed tree is missing or does not match the lockfile still heals itself before running Nx, exactly as it does today.
- A check in this repository's suite fails when the Nx version the wrapper actually runs differs from the version `package.json` pins, and names both versions when it fails.
- That check reads the version from a real wrapper invocation rather than from the wrapper's source text.
- A journey under `tests/e2e/` drives the real wrapper end to end and proves the Nx it ran is the pinned one.
- The wrapper's contract for its callers is unchanged: the preserved log, the shared cache key it exports, the success line, the failure line and its exit codes are what they were.
- The repository's complete gate is green over the finished tree.
- The dispatch closes with a completion report naming what was verified and the evidence for each claim.

### Operational notes for this host

**Iterate on the judged tier alone. Never loop on the complete gate.** This is the single
most expensive mistake made in this workstream: one node ran the complete gate three times
to learn its lint findings — ~28 minutes a round, each round ending on the judged tier
after the deterministic tier had already passed — and then cleared its last two findings in
four minutes once it split them. Your loop is

    just lint-llm-diff "$BASE"

alone, about two minutes a roll. The complete gate is `complete_gate` below, and you run it
over the **finished** tree to confirm rather than as the loop that finds your findings.
What that "once" does and does not license is the paragraph after next.

**Define the complete gate once, before you start, and never spell it out again.** Every
part of it varies by repository — the base branch is not always `main`, the recipe that is
the full bar is not always called `gate`, and that recipe already runs the judged tier in
some repositories while in others that tier is a separate step — so all of it lives in one
definition and everything below calls it. **Derive both values before you run anything;
neither is a fixed string, and the second one is the one workers get wrong:**

    BASE=origin/master   # confirm it: git remote show origin | sed -n 's/.*HEAD branch: /origin\//p'

                         # this repository's full bar, whatever it is called

you are meant to do: crozier has none, and its `check` is described by its own `just --list`
as *"Full quality gate. Fails on any issue."* — so `GATE=check` there, and a dispatch that
insisted on `just gate` would have run nothing at all.

carried a per-identity `gate:` command until **onevcs 0.11.0 removed the concept** — a rule
is `{publication, approvals}` now and a `gate:` key is refused by name — so it is no longer
an answer. `just repos`'s gate column is not one either: it is the registry's own detection
from the origin and the checkout, and it prints `just gate` for repositories that have no
such recipe. The repository's own `just --list` is what decides.

It has to run as **one invocation**, over the tree you are reporting on. That is the whole
of what is being checked — that the chain ran end to end in one command, not that your
report echoes this file's spelling of it. A report that **names the command you
substituted** (`just bootstrap && just check && just lint-llm-diff origin/master`) has
satisfied the rule, and is the better report, because it says what actually ran. What fails
is running the parts separately, however green each was on its own — which is why nothing
below ever names a part of the chain instead of the whole of it.

**"Once" is a rule against looping, not a per-dispatch budget.** The reason to run the
complete gate exactly once is that it is a ~28-minute way to learn something the judged
tier reports in two; it is not an allowance of one run per dispatch to be spent and then
cited. A worker today read it as the budget, edited a file after its gate had gone green,
and would have cited that green in its completion report — correctly, by the letter of the
instruction, which is why the instruction is now stated in full. A gate run that predates
your last edit verified a tree that no longer exists, and a report citing it is inaccurate
however green it was. So: iterate on the judged tier alone, then run the complete gate over
the tree you are actually reporting on. If it reports something, fix that and run it again
— that second run is the rule working, not a breach of it. What you may never do is reach
for it *before* the judged tier, to discover findings, which is the whole cost above.

**Never signal a process you did not identify by PID, and a PID you got from a pattern is
still a pattern kill.** Several managers share this host, and their dispatches, drivers,
publications and test servers run under the same few binary names — `just`, `node`,
`python`, `onepipeline-api` — so a kill by name knows nothing about *whose* work it
matched. The distinction is the tool rather than the pattern: `pgrep` and `ps` **read**,
and either spelling of them is fine, `pgrep -x` included; `pkill` **signals**, and it is
never the answer here, in any spelling. `-x` is the trap, because it reads as the careful
one — `pkill -f 'just gate'` at least needs a narrowing pattern, while `pkill -x just`
takes every `just` on the machine. Reading the table first and piping the pids into `kill`
is no way around it: that is the same pattern kill with more steps.

Two workers reached that place from different directions on 2026-08-24, while another
manager's dispatch had been live over an hour. One ran `pkill -TERM -x just`. The other
ran `ps -eo pid,args | grep 'onepipeline-api serve' | awk '{print $1}' | while read pid;
do kill "$pid"; done` — which obeys the letter of every paragraph below and does the same
damage, because `just dag-ui` and the e2e suites both spawn that server and a pytest run's
were alive at that moment.

**The one process you may signal is one you started yourself, so capture its PID as you
start it:**

    cmd & MYPID=$!
    kill "$MYPID"

Anything you did not start belongs to somebody. Read what it is, report what you found,
and leave it running.

**A wait written against a full command line never ends, because one of those command
lines is yours.** That is a different defect from the one above — it wedges your own
dispatch rather than somebody else's — and it is why `pgrep -f` cannot be waited on.
`pgrep -f` matches its pattern against every process's whole argv and excludes exactly one
process — itself — never the shell that invoked it. So any pattern naming the thing you are
waiting for is, by construction, a substring of the command line of the shell doing the
waiting: `until ! pgrep -f "just gate"` matches its own loop and never exits, and so does
the same loop written against `llmlint-judge.sh`, `scripts/fetch-corpus.sh`, or
`publish-branch`. That is a defect in the polling mechanism rather than a fact about gates,
so it applies to every wait you write.

That has wedged four workers here, and then two more workers and the manager itself in one
night: seven instances of one defect. A crozier corpus audit waited in `until ! pgrep -f
'scripts/fetch-corpus.sh'` with no fetch running at all — the only two matches were its own
polling shell and the manager's diagnostic shell — and waited until it was interrupted. A
`check-plan-bar-conflict` dispatch waited on `! pgrep -f "llmlint-judge.sh"`, whose negation
could never become true, and was cancelled and killed; its replacement then reached for
`pkill -f` against three patterns, which is not a wait at all but the same self-match with a
signal attached, and is refused above. And the manager, an hour after instructing a worker
about this, guarded a launch with `pgrep -f "publish-branch" && echo ABORT || launch`, whose
pattern was a literal substring of the launching shell's own command line: it aborted
unconditionally and then reported a publish as RUNNING that did not exist. That last one is
the evidence that matters most — a rule its own author reproduces an hour after issuing it
is a rule whose wording is the problem rather than its reader.

**Wait with a sentinel file.** Background `complete_gate` itself — the whole chain, so what
you waited on is the same command the paragraphs above call complete — and poll for a file
only that command can write:

    ( complete_gate > /tmp/gate.log 2>&1; echo $? > /tmp/gate.exit ) &
    until [ -f /tmp/gate.exit ]; do sleep 20; done

**To ask whether a process is running at all, match the executable, not the command line.**
`pgrep -x onepipeline` matches process *names* exactly — the binary, not its arguments — so
the shell doing the asking, whose own name is `bash`, cannot match it however the pattern
is spelled. Where the binary name is not distinctive enough to identify what you mean
(`just`, `node` and `python` run everything), read the process table instead and drop the
one self-match that form has:

    ps -eo pid,args | grep -v grep | grep 'lint-llm-diff'

the tool signals. The replacement for the worker wedged above reached for `pkill -f "just
gate"`, `pkill -f "just check"` and `pkill -f "nx run"` while another manager's run was
live. Read to learn what is running, report what you found, and signal nothing you did not
start.

**One sentinel and one log per invocation, and look before you launch one.** That pair is a
shape rather than two literal paths. Several dispatches run on this host at once and they
share `/tmp`, so a second worker writing `/tmp/gate.log` writes into the first one's — and

and check that nothing is already in flight before starting one. Three workers collided on
shared names today and not one of the three failures read as what it was: two
deterministic-tier runs deadlocked against the same cargo target-directory lock, so both
logs sat unchanged and neither progressed — about fifteen minutes lost and three
interruptions to a live turn; two whole-e2e runs wrote to one log, and stopping the
duplicate left four `SIGTERM` entries in it that read exactly like real test failures; two
judged-tier runs raced and wasted a roll, which was harmless only by luck. Read a log that
has stopped growing as two commands blocking each other before you read it as one command
working.

**Root-owned files after a container run.** The pre-push visual guard captures in Docker
as root and can leave `.nx/` and `dist/` unwritable, failing the *next* gate with `NX
Permission denied (os error 13)`. There is no passwordless sudo; repair from inside a
container:

    docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble \
      chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /w

**If a test fails in a way that makes no sense, check the host before the test.** On
2026-08-19 two publication attempts against the same already-green branch failed on two
unrelated tests — a 5-second timeout, then a browser remote that never came up — and both
were written up as flakes. The host was at 197G/197G, and the next attempt said so
outright with `No space left on device`. A full disk does not announce itself to a test
runner; it announces itself as an unrelated test failing. One command rules it out:

    df -h /home .

**The judged tier is nondeterministic.** It has already returned opposite verdicts on an
identical diff in this workstream. Clear the findings it names, then stop — do not re-run
hunting a clean sheet, and never suppress a rule to move a number. If a rule looks wrong
or misapplied, say so with evidence rather than editing it.

**`--no-verify` is not an acceptable response to a slow or inconvenient hook.** The hooks
are this repository's enforcement point — there is no CI — so bypassing one commits work
that nothing has checked, and the closeout gate does not catch it afterwards: that runs
over the finished tree, by which point a bypassed commit is simply history. Two workers
today reached for `git commit --no-verify`, both on a commit they had judged mechanical,
and one of the two was a *merge* commit — a conflict resolution, which is the single most
likely commit in a dispatch to be wrong. No gate caught either one; the monitor caught
both. If a hook is slow, wait for it. If it refuses, it is telling you something about the
commit in front of you, and the answer is to fix the commit.

**Publication goes through the harness.** No `git push`, no `gh pr create`, no `gh pr
merge`. Finish the branch, commit everything, leave the tree clean, and report — the
lifecycle publishes it after you settle. Publication is explicitly **not** yours to
perform and **not** part of your acceptance criteria.

### State the bar in `## Acceptance criteria`, not only here

A judge reads this node's `## Acceptance criteria` and its own review bar. Where the
criteria are silent about something the bar demands, it imports the demand and applies its
own reading of it — and finished, gate-green work has been failed twice that way: once for
running the gate's parts separately, and once for never having *"provided a final verified
completion report"*, a demand in neither the task nor the shared completion clause.

So every demand this node will be held to is stated as a criterion of its own, including
the two the bar makes of every implementation dispatch:

- the behavior this node adds is **proven end to end** by a test or journey that drives the
  real interface, rather than by inspection;
- the dispatch closes with a **final completion report** naming what was verified and the
  evidence for it.

Criteria state properties of the finished tree; the commands that produce them belong in
this section. `just check-plan <plan.json>` refuses a task whose criteria omit a demand its
resolved review bar — or this appendix — makes of it.

## What

Root cause 10 in the issue says the Nx computation cache is workspace-local here and
prescribes deleting `nx.json`'s cache-directory line. **That prescription is wrong for this
repository, and a dispatch that followed it would change nothing and report success.**
Measured on this host on 2026-08-26, and re-measure it yourself rather than taking it on
trust:

- `scripts/nx.sh` already exports `NX_CACHE_DIRECTORY` to
  `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/ai-orchestrator/nx/<first 16 hex of the sha256 of the
  origin url>`, which overrides `nx.json` on every path that goes through the wrapper.
- `.nx/cache` does not exist in this checkout at all; `.nx` holds only `workspace-data` and
  the llmlint-diff state.
- The canonical checkout, both isolated clones and a live `onevcs` run clone all resolve to
  the same key, `756e79f93796751d`, which holds 80 MB and served a recorded
  `local-cache-hit` on 2026-08-25. So a publication clone already shares the cache a
  session worktree earned, by directory.

Two things there are real, and this step owes an answer on each.

**The empty keys.** The cache root holds 161 key directories of which only four are
non-empty. The key falls back to `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` when a checkout has no
`origin` remote — which is what the e2e journeys' copies of this checkout are — so each such
copy mints a private key directory that is created by the wrapper and then never used.
Decide whether that is litter worth removing at the source, and either change it or record
why it stays and what removes it.

**The cost.** The issue's "roughly 37 minutes of gate" was measured against something other
than the cause it names, so the figure cannot be carried forward. Re-measure a
publication-shaped run of the complete gate against this wrapper — what replays, what
re-runs, and why each miss missed — and record that figure with what produced it.

Then correct this repository's own prose wherever it would lead the next reader to the
issue's conclusion, and make whatever change the measurement justifies. A measurement that
justifies no change to the caching itself is a complete answer, provided the answer is
recorded where the next reader will find it.

Confine your edits in `AGENTS.md` to the paragraphs about `scripts/nx.sh`, the Nx cache and
the workspace install. Two sibling nodes are editing other regions of that file
concurrently, and keeping the regions disjoint is what keeps three branches auto-mergeable.

## Why

Nick is paying the gate cost on the critical path of every change, and reached for a fix
that this repository had already made — which is worse than having no fix, because it reads
as done. The next person to open root cause 10 needs the measurement rather than the
prescription, and nothing currently records which of the two is true here.

## Acceptance criteria

- The recorded answer names where the Nx computation cache lives at run time for this repository, which configuration decides it, and whether a publication clone shares the cache a session worktree earned — each with the measurement behind it.
- The empty-key question is answered: either the wrapper no longer mints a key directory for a checkout that has no origin remote, or this repository's prose records why those directories are correct and what removes them.
- The gate cost the issue attributes to a workspace-local cache is re-measured against this wrapper, and the recorded figure names what replayed, what re-ran, and why.
- No sentence left in this repository's prose would lead a reader to change `nx.json`'s cache-directory setting expecting an effect on what the wrapper does.
- Any behaviour this step changes in the wrapper is proven end to end by a journey under `tests/e2e/` that drives the real wrapper against real Nx.
- The repository's complete gate is green over the finished tree.
- The dispatch closes with a completion report naming what was verified and the evidence for each claim.

tasks.task:
## What

`onepipeline adopt <RUN>` accepts no flags. `src/cli.rs` declares it as `Adopt(RunArgs)`,
and `RunArgs` carries a run id and nothing else, while `--attach` and `--detach` are on
`StartArgs` alone. So an adopting launch cannot be detached — it is refused with `unexpected
argument '--detach'` — and a manager who must stay responsive is pushed into backgrounding
the process by hand, which this host's operating doctrine otherwise spends a paragraph
forbidding.

meaning. `start --detach` in `src/driver.rs` already has the shape to follow: it writes the
launch record durably *before* anything that reads it exists, disowns its standard handles
so the retained driver does not hold the launcher's streams, retains this same executable at
the hidden drive verb, and waits for that process to claim the run before printing — so a
driver that died on its way up is reported with what it said rather than printed as a live
pid.

ownership, refuses a run something is still driving, displaces a driver holding a run
nothing is driving, and takes the engine lock before writing its record. A detaching
adoption must not hold that lock on behalf of the process that will actually drive, and

false negative.** `src/sys.rs`'s `platform_process_start_token` records it as `ps -o
lstart=` — a rendered wall-clock string — and `StartToken::matches` compares by exact string
equality. `ps` does not store that rendering on Linux; it reconstructs it, and the
reconstruction moves under clock discipline. Measured over one session on one live process:
`01:33:06` read at about 01:38, `01:33:01` at about 01:47, `01:33:00` at about 01:52; a
controlled probe on the same pid 75 seconds apart gave `01:33:00` then `01:32:59`. About one
second of drift per 75 seconds, backwards.

Reproduced end to end against a scratch runs root and a `sleep` process, launching no run —
same pid, same process, only the token's age differing. With a token read three minutes
earlier the stop reported `{"stopped":true,"teardown":"nothing-to-stop"}` and said the pid
had since been given to another process, and the process **survived**; with a token read
seconds earlier the same stop killed it. It explains the originating incident exactly: a
record whose token was written at 18:02:18, corroborated by the journal's own
`driver-adopted` at 18:02:19.414Z, read as 18:01:45 sixty-eight minutes later — 33 seconds
backwards, the measured direction and order of magnitude. Four alternatives were tested and
disproved first: that adoption updates the pid without the token, that the reader's TZ or
locale skewed it, that the record was stale, and that the record was wrong.

verifying as they age. Every launch record is older than 75 seconds within two minutes of a
run starting, so in practice no liveness claim against a real run is verifiable. A
long-running driver becomes unstoppable, the run keeps its identity hold, `onepipeline start`
then refuses new runs on that identity — observed twice — and the operator is pushed toward
signalling processes by pattern on a host several managers share. `claim_on` in
`src/driver.rs` is the reader, and its `Reissued` answer, "a live process this host says is
not the one the record named", is exactly what a drifted token produces. Check whether the
`stale repository holder ... proceeding` line printed on every launch shares the same
comparison; if it does, this is a correctness problem in the concurrency guard and not only
in the stop path.

and the change must make that argument rather than sidestep it.** The doc comment above
`platform_process_start_token` considers `/proc/<pid>/stat` and rejects it by name: `ps` is
the deliberate portability compromise, because "a platform fixed in only one of them" is
what a second implementation buys, and macOS has no `/proc`. The report's own suggestion —
compare with a **tolerance** rather than by string equality — engages that argument on its
own terms and is the safer starting point.

- The drift is a **rate**, not an offset. A tolerance small enough to keep pid reuse honest
  at a minute is useless against a record an hour old, so a tolerance fix has to scale with
  the record's age — a strictly larger design than the report implies.

  understood to render a start time the kernel stores at process creation, while Linux's
  `ps` re-derives it from the current clock less uptime — which is precisely the mechanism
  the measurements above show, and is consistent with `/proc/stat`'s `btime` having been
  byte-identical across every read on the day `ps` wandered six seconds. If that is so, a
  kernel-fixed reading on Linux fixes the only broken platform and leaves the sound one on
  the path it was always right on, which **inverts** the portability objection rather than
  merely disagreeing with it.

own `ps` does — do not inherit it from this task.** If it is false, this node still owes a
recorded identity that does not decay, by whatever means it then argues for. Whichever route
is taken, state the argument and the trade-off in the change, including what it costs
against pid reuse.

live.** This is independent of the token and stands whatever happens to it. `stop` already
refuses honestly for three teardown outcomes — nothing attempted, partly signalled, and
every ask refused — but a walk that *found* live processes and declined every one of them,
because their recorded identities disagreed, folds to the same "nothing to aim at" answer as
a run whose work was genuinely already over, prints `stopped: true`, and exits 0. That

`carry_hooks` in `crates/onevcs/src/git.rs` — at line 847 on `main` today, and
byte-identical to the line 715 the report quotes — gives a disposable publication clone the
*lender's* hooks. A relative `core.hooksPath` is resolved against `source`, so a lender
configured with `core.hooksPath = .husky` points every clone at `<lender>/.husky`: the
registered checkout's working tree, sitting on its base branch. The hook that runs is
therefore whichever version is checked out in the lender, never the one the branch ships.

directory, the clone is pointed at `<lender>/.githooks`.

## What

An agent turn served by codex records no normalized tool events, so the run journal goes
blind exactly where a manager most needs it. Across 117 recorded runs carrying attribution,
keyed on the explicitly labelled agent-side entry: codex-only agent side, 2 runs, both with
zero `turn-activity`; claude-code only, 110 runs, none; mixed, 5 runs, none, because the
claude-code turns supply it. Localised by comparing two turns' own history files from the
same graph and worktree layout — the claude-code agent turn carried 348 `event` records and
the codex one carried none at all, so nothing downstream had anything to relay. That
contradicts this crate's own `--events` help text, which says harnesses whose default
already carries a transcript, Codex among them, report events regardless. Two controls rule
out the obvious alternatives: the affected run already ran on the current stack, and an
independent codex-only run from the previous day with no refusals at all was also zero.

**The report calls this "codex-served turns", and the real predicate is narrower and more
damaging: it is a *controlled* turn.** `ControlShape::CodexAppServer` drives a controlled
codex turn over the `codex app-server` JSON-RPC protocol rather than over `codex exec
--json`, and this crate's own note says oneharness drives the turn itself over the
mechanism's protocol for every shape **except** Claude Code, which rides its ordinary
headless run — which is exactly why claude-code turns kept their events under the same

way every other recognizer here was sourced** — this module's own header says all four

    ( complete_gate > /tmp/gate.log 2>&1; echo $? > /tmp/gate.exit ) &
    until [ -f /tmp/gate.exit ]; do sleep 20; done

**To ask whether a process is running at all, match the executable, not the command line.**
`pgrep -x onepipeline` matches process *names* exactly — the binary, not its arguments — so
the shell doing the asking, whose own name is `bash`, cannot match it however the pattern
is spelled. Where the binary name is not distinctive enough to identify what you mean
(`just`, `node` and `python` run everything), read the process table instead and drop the
one self-match that form has:

    ps -eo pid,args | grep -v grep | grep 'lint-llm-diff'

Both of those are **reads**, which is what makes `-x` safe here and forbidden the moment
the tool signals. The replacement for the worker wedged above reached for `pkill -f "just
gate"`, `pkill -f "just check"` and `pkill -f "nx run"` while another manager's run was
live. Read to learn what is running, report what you found, and signal nothing you did not
start.

**One sentinel and one log per invocation, and look before you launch one.** That pair is a
shape rather than two literal paths. Several dispatches run on this host at once and they
share `/tmp`, so a second worker writing `/tmp/gate.log` writes into the first one's — and
`until [ -f /tmp/gate.exit ]` returns immediately on somebody else's exit file, reporting
their result as yours. Name both after the invocation (`/tmp/gate.$$.log`, or the node id),
and check that nothing is already in flight before starting one. Three workers collided on
shared names today and not one of the three failures read as what it was: two
deterministic-tier runs deadlocked against the same cargo target-directory lock, so both
logs sat unchanged and neither progressed — about fifteen minutes lost and three
interruptions to a live turn; two whole-e2e runs wrote to one log, and stopping the
duplicate left four `SIGTERM` entries in it that read exactly like real test failures; two
judged-tier runs raced and wasted a roll, which was harmless only by luck. Read a log that
has stopped growing as two commands blocking each other before you read it as one command
working.

**Root-owned files after a container run.** The pre-push visual guard captures in Docker
as root and can leave `.nx/` and `dist/` unwritable, failing the *next* gate with `NX
Permission denied (os error 13)`. There is no passwordless sudo; repair from inside a
container:

    docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble \
      chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /w

**If a test fails in a way that makes no sense, check the host before the test.** On
2026-08-19 two publication attempts against the same already-green branch failed on two
unrelated tests — a 5-second timeout, then a browser remote that never came up — and both
were written up as flakes. The host was at 197G/197G, and the next attempt said so
outright with `No space left on device`. A full disk does not announce itself to a test
runner; it announces itself as an unrelated test failing. One command rules it out:

    df -h /home .

**The judged tier is nondeterministic.** It has already returned opposite verdicts on an
identical diff in this workstream. Clear the findings it names, then stop — do not re-run
hunting a clean sheet, and never suppress a rule to move a number. If a rule looks wrong
or misapplied, say so with evidence rather than editing it.

**`--no-verify` is not an acceptable response to a slow or inconvenient hook.** The hooks
are this repository's enforcement point — there is no CI — so bypassing one commits work
that nothing has checked, and the closeout gate does not catch it afterwards: that runs
over the finished tree, by which point a bypassed commit is simply history. Two workers
today reached for `git commit --no-verify`, both on a commit they had judged mechanical,
and one of the two was a *merge* commit — a conflict resolution, which is the single most
likely commit in a dispatch to be wrong. No gate caught either one; the monitor caught
both. If a hook is slow, wait for it. If it refuses, it is telling you something about the
commit in front of you, and the answer is to fix the commit.

**Publication goes through the harness.** No `git push`, no `gh pr create`, no `gh pr
merge`. Finish the branch, commit everything, leave the tree clean, and report — the
lifecycle publishes it after you settle. Publication is explicitly **not** yours to
perform and **not** part of your acceptance criteria.

### State the bar in `## Acceptance criteria`, not only here

A judge reads this node's `## Acceptance criteria` and its own review bar. Where the
criteria are silent about something the bar demands, it imports the demand and applies its
own reading of it — and finished, gate-green work has been failed twice that way: once for
running the gate's parts separately, and once for never having *"provided a final verified
completion report"*, a demand in neither the task nor the shared completion clause.

So every demand this node will be held to is stated as a criterion of its own, including
the two the bar makes of every implementation dispatch:

- the behavior this node adds is **proven end to end** by a test or journey that drives the
  real interface, rather than by inspection;
- the dispatch closes with a **final completion report** naming what was verified and the
  evidence for it.

Criteria state properties of the finished tree; the commands that produce them belong in
this section. `just check-plan <plan.json>` refuses a task whose criteria omit a demand its
resolved review bar — or this appendix — makes of it.
